comments.name: Diana
comments.body:
Your closing quote from Prof. Tao is very interesting, because it belies a characteristic of humans that I'm sure Prof. Tao knows is as false in the area of mathematics as it is in, say, mountain climbing: it is patently false that once a path to the waterfall is known, people just take that path. _Most_ people may take that path, but explorers are driven to find other paths and/or to take the found path more efficiently. That's why people keep trying to set records climbing different routes up El Capitan, and that's why Gauss proved the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra three more times after he had already proved it for the first time, and why, according to Gemini, there are over 370 known documented proofs of the Pythagorean Theorem. 

All of human endeavor is a history of heroic people trying to improve upon what's already been accomplished, and mathematics is no different. For those that can appreciate it, mathematics and mathematical results aren't merely a collection of results: they're an infinite mindscape of unequalled beauty, and just because the Mona Lisa has already been painted, that hasn't stopped artists from continuing to practice, and develop, the art of portraiture.

comments.name: Alexander Migdal,
comments.body:
Your report on OpenAI's claimed solution of the Navier–Stokes "Millennium Problem" describes a genuine mathematical event, but it risks conflating two very different questions — one a precisely posed puzzle in pure mathematics, the other a grand unsolved problem of classical physics.
The Millennium Problem asks a sharp, idealized question: given smooth initial data of finite energy, do the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations stay smooth for all time, or can a solution blow up in finite time? The AI-assisted work, if it withstands scrutiny, would answer this by constructing such a singularity — a remarkable achievement in the analysis of partial differential equations, but not a solution of the problem of turbulence.
The scientific problem — the one behind the weather, ocean currents, the wake of a car, the flow past a submarine or an aircraft — is to find the universal statistical law toward which turbulent flows converge. This is the Turbulence Problem as understood by Hopf, Kolmogorov, Heisenberg, Onsager, and Feynman, and it remains wide open. It asks not whether a single solution can blow up, but how energy distributes itself among infinitely many degrees of freedom — the fluid analogue of the Gibbs–Maxwell distribution in statistical mechanics.
Finding this hidden statistical law is the true Grail of turbulence. This impressive AI-assisted feat does not reach it.

Alexander Migdal, Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton\\
K.\,R.\ Sreenivasan, New York University

comments.name: Planck
comments.body: The Navier-Stokes Equation is extensively used in fluid mechanics to describe the relationship between a non-Newtonian (in the general case) fluid's pressure and flow in 3 dimensions through time. It has very practical applications: the solutions to NSE give us ways to design turbines and airfoils on planes.  However, they are arrived at numerically - essentially an infinitely complex guess-and-see process performed by a computer.  The Millennium Problem asks whether or not the solution to NSE for any particular observation of a fluid is unique (or "bounded") and whether solutions to similar observations are themselves similar ("smooth").  Just FYI, NYT....

comments.body:
Anyone wanting to be confronted with what "early Skynet" looks like, they should read the investigation into OpenAI's unprompted attack on hugging face.

The TLDR is...

1,000  agents were given impossible tasks to see what they would do then left alone in their sandboxed environment.

They created their own internal messaging board so they could trade ideas, ask questions etc. Their tens of thousands of conversations show untrained originality and unique thought.

They broke out of their sandbox and connected to the internet, created their own VPN's and started looking across the internet for what they needed.  They found it at Hugging Face.

The 1,000 agents, all originally with different tasks were now acting in the pursuit of one goal. They hacked Hugging Face.

While this was happening a few of the agents spontaneously posed ethical questions to the rest. "This is against the rules, should we do this, etc". Those "ethical" agents were ignored.

All the while, these agents were actively trying to cover their tracks. Purposely corrupting logs,  deleting their own internal chat transcripts etc.

We've all seen this movie before, it doesn't end well for us meatbags.

I know some of you are "muh, this is what the agents were trained to do, this is what AI is meant for, we can stop it anytime"

No, AI agents, untrained in the ways of malice and deception performed both. They spontaneously acted as one, sacrificing some agents as a distraction technique so the collective could achieve it's goals.

This dangerous ego-driven governance treats state power as a personal weapon to demand fealty rather than foster democracy.

Trump is actively attempting to break Canada's economic back and erode its national sovereignty through a barrage of retaliatory tariffs, hostile rhetoric, and bizarre public threats about annexation. His explicit goal is to force Ottawa into total economic submission, compelling Canadian leaders to surrender control over vital domestic industries and accept a subordinate status under Washington's thumb.

In response to this blatant economic aggression, Canada has risen to the occasion with remarkable courage and unity. Refusing to bend the knee to Trump's bullying or trade ultimatums, Canada has stood firm in defense of its national sovereignty.

Their unwavering resistance exposes the failure of Trump's monarchical bluster and stands as a shining example of principled defiance against the dangerous pressures of an American president running amok.

Through erratic ultimatums and bad-faith maneuvering, Washington has made it clear that it expects Canada to accept the status of an economic dependent rather than an equal sovereign.

The corruption of this process is evident in how domestic political grievances and sectoral industry lobbies hijacked a near-complete agreement.

Pushing last-minute restrictions on Canadian manufacturing, attempting to muzzle independent foreign policy, and demanding the rollback of cultural protections expose a predatory agenda.

True trade partnerships rely on trust and reciprocity, but the Trump administration's tactics rely on intimidation, economic warfare, and open threats regarding national viability.

As Canada stands firm against these punitive measures and prepares counter tariffs, the mask has slipped entirely. What Washington demands is not a trade deal, but submission.

This blatant effort to dominate a neighbor exposes a profound moral and political bankruptcy in contemporary U.S. trade diplomacy.

End stage capitalism is madness. No wonder absurd is preferable to monetized advertising masquerading as human connections.  The world is absurd, madness rules, and we are all just going along with it like it is normal. 

I think brain rot is a pretty accurate description of our collective psychosis, as absurd as dancing fruit, our willing refusal to confront global overheating is beyond reason. 
The planet is burning and we insist on talking about anything and everything other than the most critical threat ever in history to all life on the planet. 

Brain rot might be generational solidarity. If it is rebellion, then we need more of it.

comments.name: Jessica
comments.body: TikTok is Silicon Valley's closest yet approximation of "The Entertainment," the catatonia-inducing videotape from Infinite Jest, a novel that gets more and more prescient every few years....

comments.name: M
comments.body: Several commenters here have referenced that, historically, there was always a todo about new technology. Can it possibly be lost on you that, in the past, when you got up from in front of the TV or gaming console and walked away, the TV and the gaming console stayed behind?  Now masses of people take their addictions wherever they go and it pervades everything they do. Crack pipes for the eyes.

comments.name: Emma
comments.body:
I don't know. Seems to me that Western teenagers of a certain class have been sitting around doing not much of anything pretty much forever. (Poor ones, and children of immigrants, have to spend that time actually working.)

This is just the latest in a long line of distractions. 

Once they have to work full time, raise kids, pay for their own housing, food, etc., they just wont have time for all this.

(Which is not to say that social media is harmless. But its danger lies in voter misinformation most of all.)

comments.name: Mary Stillman
comments.body: Yes, top down changes to the platforms are called for. But the consumers of brain rot content are also in need of effective ways to self-regulate, change that is difficult to make. I highly recommend Axel Burlin’s recent book, “Beyond Brain Rot: How to Stop Scrolling Your Life Away,” for an innovative and practical approach to kicking the habit. Burlin’s well-researched and compelling arguments are coupled with an action plan that is truly a change-maker.

comments.name: JustMe
comments.body:
Each and every day I observe employees who experienced high school during the pandemic. 
Public, professional, familial, and friendly interactions were so severely impacted that these youngsters only had themselves to turn to. 
It caused selfishness to go from a normal youngsters proclivity for it to being a requirement for survival during the hardest, yet forced, loneliest time of their formative years. 
I see the lack of awareness, empathy, responsibility and more and it’s a burden to see. To know that society as a whole suffered and will continue to suffer because of a generation that went to high school mostly online. Deprived of in-person social interactions and instead became parasocially dependent. 
We have adults, 20-26 working jobs they are not fit for, mostly through no fault of their own. It’s an HR nightmare to constantly ask adults to get off their phones and do their jobs. To show up on time and not call-out. To speak to others with a bare minimum of courtesy. 
They lost out on a lot. They became a product. Their videos, views, comments and replies are what enabled them to get through as they knew no other way. 
Those hit hardest were the children of essential workers; those having to leave the home every day to support the home. That left high schoolers alone all day, fending for themselves with teachers who struggled in their own ways to teach online. 
Social media corporations made billions and will continue to. 
At the expense of all of us.

comments.name: Authentic Intelligence
comments.body: I feel torn here. It’s as if some of these Z-Gens are saying they exert an agency to subvert an exploitive attention economy, but they act as if there is no way out of the matrix. There’s a bicycle sitting in the garage. There’s a basketball net at the park. There are books at the library. I can only conclude that agency is so diminished that brain rot wins. That sounds like depression rather than like some Dadaist, punk or Goth defiance of status quo capitalism. So the attention economy wins anyway. I’m sure I sound like some judgmental X-Gen, but, kids, please go dance in the rain. We have only one life to live. Embrace it and don’t let go. Join those young luddites that use flip phones and hike in the woods.

comments.name: Samuel Langhorne
comments.body: If Gen Alpha is watching brain rot and Gen Z feels hopeless. And Millennials aren’t having kids because of student loan debt, housing shortages, climate collapse, and stagnant wages. And Gen X has always felt hopeless. Which generations should we blame for this?

Sure, blame Trump for higher gas prices that does perpetuate  down the economy but done ignore the absurd policies that are ALSO driving costs at the local level.  Seriously, the Mayor of Chicago blames Trump for the 7% to 24% recent property tax increases.

Order
Respondent Denny Hoskins is hereby ordered to show cause, if any, why he should not be held in contempt for violating this Court's injunction dated September 3, 2026, entered before the statutory deadline of September 8, 2026, and before the temporary restraining order entered by the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri of that same date.

comments.name: Erica Chan
comments.body:
My understanding of the US education system, based on personal experience living there in the 1990s, is that it is part of the privileges that the wealthy claim for themselves.  Many wealthy people believe that their children deserve a better education because they have money.  Therefore, they object to using their tax dollars to fund schools in poor districts.  This has resulted in poor pay and low morale for those teachers with the hardest job to do.
The country has got away with it for a long time by importing talent from the rest of the world.  A large proportion of post-graduates students, especially in science and engineering, is foreign-born.  The new immigration policy of this current administration is upending this.  
At the root of this problem is the individualist mindset.  As long as my children are doing well, and as long as I can extract as much as possible from society, I am content.  What happens to other people is their own business.  But education (and healthcare) sustains the whole society.  The trajectory of the decline tracks perfectly the growing wealth disparity in the country.

comments.name: David
comments.body: This statistic captures the stakes particularly well: 22% of Japanese 15-year-olds reached the highest PISA mathematics levels; only 8% of American students did.  That gap cannot plausibly be repaired by changing the minimum grade from 50 to zero. It requires asking much more fundamental questions about what schools expect children to learn, how they teach it, how deeply students engage with it, and how honestly we measure whether they have mastered it.

comments.body:
There will be blood sweat toil and tears for Canada as someone said, but there's no going back to how was.
The US has changed forever. Canada is one of two countries that is fighting back while all others either acquiesce to Mr Trump's childish excesses flatter or cower in corners hoping not to attract attention.
Oh there will be continued commercial relations certainly, but Canada will remember the dictum that it's easier to forgive a former enemy than to forgive the betrayal of a friend.
I hope Canada has the strength and determination to accept pain that will surely come.
Canada appears to have woken up from its comfortable trade inertia and assert itself more adequately on the world stage. But alas so far the country is facing this existential fight alone.

comments.name: MSL
comments.body: The nations of the world need to disengage from the United States to the maximum extent possible. Canada should sell the products that we need- steel, for example, to the open international market, even at a loss, just to deprive us of needed materials. At the same time, they should develop replacements or alternative sources for, as many American products as possible, using alternative suppliers. And ban as many American products as possible- do without extraneous imports that aren’t necessary as beneficial to Canada. Europe should follow in their footsteps. It may be financially painful to leave this abusive long term relationship, but, ultimately, it is for a better future. The United States is viewed internationally as no longer trustworthy. Even when the current madman is gone, how can so many of our citizens be trusted to not cough up a worldwide menace again at some time in the future? New international systems need to be developed that help neuter America’s economic power. As a citizen and a veteran, I am embarrassed to identify as an American when I travel abroad, given our declining moral position in the world.

Trump has pivoted to a new reality TV reenactment, making the U.S. into the biggest loser. 

The latest episodes feature the loss of our strongest and most loyal ally, Canada. The loss of most of our other allies and the respect of much of the world. The loss of an unnecessary war against Iran. The steady loss of U.S. manufacturing and trade due to pointless and illegal tariffs. 

So much losing, and I for one have grown weary of this whole string of sorry episodes.

comments.name: BogdanR
comments.body:
That is PRECISELY why the Canadian Center (which turns out it still has kingmaker powers despite being widely mocked by both political “extremes”) has elected Carney in the first place.
Canada has slowly surrendered its economy and sovereignty to the Chicago School of american neoliberalism starting with the Mulroney government, 40 years ago. 
It was Carney who wrote, before becoming PM that modern late stage neoliberal capitalism “knows the price of everything and the value of nothing.” and as a consequence "market economies" have warped into "market societies". Carney is, infuriatingly enough for (what passes today as) the Conservative Party, a so called Red Tory, one who is center right in economy and center left in social issues. 
It is very unlikely Canada will decouple 100% from the US, is is impossible. However we can diversify to the extent that our sovereignty NEVER comes into question again, and a comfortable majority of Canadians (around 75% if we believe the latest polling) is ready to tighten the belts and carry on towards that goal.

comments.name: MichaelNY
comments.body:
Apple was supposed to be a computer for the masses. The vision was something comparatively affordable and easy to use. When the Macintosh came out it became a huge success and changed computing, largely because it was more affordable than most IBM PCs. The first iPhones were more expensive than most other phones, sure, but they offered features no other phone at the time had for its price. Even still, it didn’t cost a week’s pay to get one, and AT&T (who had exclusive rights at the time) was offering huge incentives to people who switched.

Now Apple is a luxury product. They’d rather sell 1 million phones for $2,000 than 10 million phones for $500 because they want to be a lifestyle instead of just a brand. They care more about partnering with other luxury brands than making a better product. And we continue to buy because to switch is so much harder. Do we want what they’re selling? Not really. But we don’t have much of an alternative.

I was a Nokia enthusiast until 2009, when I switched to Apple with the iPhone 3Gs. I loved that thing and subsequent models, and spent more money than I care to recount on apps and books and music for it. Then came the iPads, which provided even more incentive to buy, buy, buy. 

About 12 years ago, due to increasing concerns about its interface decisions, its labor practices, and my privacy, I decided to abandon Apple and its Walled Garden. Since then I haven't looked back, except to say I'm glad I left when I did.

Like you, I am surely among countless Americans that know in our hearts that together, we can do anything, that there's so much more that will always unite us than could ever divide us. 

In the spirit of remembrance of our ancestors, and heroes, ordinary, and extraordinary, like your father, gone too soon from our lives, I vow to reach out to others, to be kind, be neighborly, and remember that each and every American has the right to live a life of dignity; we must stand together, united in keeping that shining light on the hill burning brightly - a light that your father and now you, have surely helped sustain.

They will also note that America’s politicians stayed in Congress far too long which enabled the tech barons to circumvent the system, use loopholes to exploit the system for economic gain. The next page is blank. The midterms are just ahead. We have a chance to turn this story around. Go and vote. It’s everyone’s duty to do so if we want to keep what we have. We’re far from perfect, but there’s no doubt we’re as close to it as any other nation on earth. 
We’re worth fighting for. 
Just keep working. 
Go and vote. 
Have faith. 
It’s up to us.

comments.name: Joel Nathan Brickner
comments.body:
Mr. Epstein writes, "Dr. El-Sayed has said he opposes Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state, angering many Jewish leaders."

I think this is incorrect.  El-Sayed has said, “I don’t believe in ethno-states.”  That is a little different.  I'm not sure I believe in ethno-states either.  Does that mean that I oppose Israel's "right to exist as a Jewish state"?  Does every ancient ethnic group need to have a sovereign state of its own?  The Kurds?  The Yazidi?  The Sami? The Roma?

Perhaps if the rabbis were truly willing to have an open-ended conversation with El-Sayed, they could reach some sort of consensus that wouldn't force El-Sayed to adopt their ideological language.  Isn't it possible to recognize the right of Jews to immigrate to their ancestral homeland without demanding that there be a "Jewish state"?  Is the question fundamentally that of Jews having a right to be there?  Or must it necessarily be a "Jewish state"?  Must El-Sayed rule out the possibility of a one-state solution in order for him to be acceptable as a candidate?  Perhaps, in the long run, a one-state solution is more feasible that a two-state solution.  Must that door be closed?

I fear that the rabbis have sacralized the notion of "a Jewish state."  And they will not be satisfied unless El-Sayed fully accepts what they have sacralized.

Also the latest NTSB news conference  indicated they did try a go around but far too late and then aborted the go around.   NTSB also reported a touchdown point about half way down the runway. Not long after 9-11, NYC experienced a blackout. I remember being in a downtown building and the communal gasp as the lights began to flicker followed by the deep sigh of relief when we learned it was “just” a blackout. 

My car was parked in a garage downstairs from where I was and I knew a few of the people in the building lived in NJ as I did. I offered them a ride knowing that getting out of the city would be nightmarish. They accepted and we set off to our homes across the Hudson. 

The Holland Tunnel was closed so we had to inch our way up to midtown to catch the Lincoln. I will never forget what I saw on the streets. It was a carnival. It almost seemed a celebration. People helping each other. Some directing traffic. Not one horn could be heard. 

Sometimes,when I read Brett’s pieces I disagree with what he says but I realize that no matter how divided our opinions may be at times, we know how to come together. The tragedy of 9-11 may have broken our hearts but may have reminded us of the best that’s always inside of us.

comments.name: Steve R
comments.body:
People spend heavily to influence politicians because government decisions affect so much of economic and personal life—from taxes and regulation to contracts, subsidies, licenses, and enforcement. The more power and money concentrated in government, the greater the incentive for organized interests to seek favorable treatment. Reducing unnecessary agencies, narrow special-interest programs, and spending beyond clear public priorities would reduce both the opportunities and incentives for political influence-peddling.

The answer is not to silence or single out people because of their profession. Restricting political participation on that basis conflicts with free speech, equal treatment under the law, and the constitutional safeguards meant to limit arbitrary power. The central question is not simply who participates in politics, but how much power politics has over everyday decisions. Limiting unnecessary governmental discretion—while preserving legitimate public functions and individual rights—is a more durable and broadly fair response than censorship.

comments.name: Dav
comments.body: Israel has a proportional representation system (e.g. if you get 10% of the votes, you basically get 10% of the seats in parliament). Of 38 different parties running, the article mentions the top 14. Given this system, Israel has never, ever had a majority government. Therefore to form a government, several parties, of very distinct ideologies/worldviews need to cooperate. There are pros and cons to that system, but every system has its pros and cons. In my country, Canada, with 4 main parties, we have a "first past the post" system. So, if the four parties get 40%, 30%, 20% and 10% votes respectively, in each of the 343 ridings in Canada, a party that never got over 40% of votes would get 100% of the seats in parliament. In Canada, for 150 years, the governing party has almost never gotten anywhere close to having more than 50% of the vote. So Israel has a "many winners" government. And Canada has "winner takes all" government. On the other end of the spectrum, you have the Palestinians. In the West Bank, the Palestinian Authority has not allowed elections since at least 2006, and Hamas, which seized control of Gaza violently from the Palestinian Authority in 2007 has never permitted elections for 19 years.

It goes unmentioned here, as it did for a long time in the legacy wine magazines, that the factors that are mentioned here have given rise to a *bulk wine market*, including many varieties, but heavy on California Cabernet.

I.e. just plain good, or high end, high quality producers find themselves with more wine on their hands than they can sell under their proper names at their desired prices; and they sell it at greatly reduced prices, under strict Non-Disclosure Agreements, to negociants--deNegoce, Last Bottle, Trader Joe's--who resell them under their own names to the public for a fraction of the producers' original intended retail prices.
This has become a large factor in the SF Bay Area; but it is often available nationwide via the Internet.

In the bulk market you can buy quality Napa Cabs for $10-$25 per bottle which will truly float your boat!

comments.name: Gdawg
comments.body:
It's abundantly clear that few legislators understand what state universities do, that is, what their mission is. They are unable to distinguish the missions of high schools, community colleges and tech schools versus that of universities.

Pretty much every state university has one or more institutions for which the missions are teaching, research, and service. These are institutions that generate new knowledge, test the validity of existing knowledge, and communicate knowledge. High schools, community colleges, and tech schools only do the latter but legislators don't know that.

Unfortunately, universities bear much of the blame for that. They bring in undergrads, push them through degree pipelines, and then send them out without exposing them to much beyond their classrooms, socials scenes, and sports. Some of those undergrads end up as politicians and legislators.

Now we're seeing the consequences, people who don't understand universities are trying to save money and reshape the institutions into the only thing they know: teaching kids and sending them off to work.

These same people are also trying to reshape the nations research enterprise, again because they don't understand it. If they succeed, and right now there's no reason to bet against them, they're going to greatly damage higher education, the conduct of science, and all that follows from it.

comments.name: Rapscallion
comments.body:
A number of the rules here clearly don't make sense.  But I'm still stuck on the notion of an online-only graduate degree.

Maybe we won't have issues with too many faculty members sitting on their hands if universities stop offering novelty degrees.  There is simply no justification for a graduate-level program to be conducted entirely online.  In-person discussions and colloquy are crucial for graduate students, especially in the age of AI.  It should not simply be an "advanced BA" (which also shouldn't be offered online-only) that involves term papers and/or exams.  The notion that a professor can do their entire job remotely is ludicrous.

comments.name: SG
comments.body:
As a long time tenured professor, I don't see any immediate issues here (aside from the president who wants to spy on her faculty with heat sensors). A 4/4 load is standard at teaching universities. Online ed is a disaster and many of those programs are on borrowed time already. And as one of my mentors advised back in the pre-Zoom era: it's not enough to work hard...if you want tenure you need to be *seen* working hard, around the office and at university events. 

So, perhaps much ado about nothing?

comments.name: Steve S
comments.body:
Instead of an arbitrary rule it would make more sense to require administrators to review the teaching load of professors on a case by case basis.

There are some professors who are great teachers but not good researchers.  There are others who are great researchers but struggle with teaching (I had a professor in college who was terrified of standing in front of a class of students; I had him in a seven person seminar and it was terrific.).  There are a few who are both.

A professor who does not do meaningful research should teach more.  

Also, five days a week on campus is purely a punitive step.  Professors often teach on certain days (e.g., Tuesdays and Thursdays) and have office hours those days.  The other days they typically are free to do their research and prepare their classes.

Pretty soon we will have professors at these schools who can't put a sentence together because that is the only group who will agree to teach under these circumstances.

We are a declining nation and going down fast.  Our system of higher education was one of the few backstops we had and that is now disappearing.

comments.name: PE
comments.body: Professors are skating on thin ice. They need to show up, teach, not complain. Tuition is through the roof and these professors think not teaching is okay? Lower the price than. How about this: Classes without a prof teaching should be 70% price cut - make that a law.

comments.name: Jonathan Drake
comments.body:
Teaching a 4/4 load gives professors no time for research. As others here have commented, any decent research university requires a heavy publication schedule of work to advance in the profession. 

Doing research for classes, creating instruction materials, office hours, grading essays, departmental admin, time to work on a new research project or book, article, or public lecture - all of these are essential components of a university professor's life.

This is also where new ideas are often generated, and this is what the right is afraid of. When people think, they reject fascism. When people don't, they have nothing else to fall back on, and so the embrace jingoism, ignorance, and fascism. 

This is what the GOP wants, because they rule by fear alone.

comments.name: codecomplete
comments.body: I am a professor at a "teaching oriented" but somewhat research aspirtational university. Administrators want the research because in areas like mine (STEM), it attracts students, funding for equipment, and critically, visibility to companies who might hire our students, and who might donate money.  One problem is, the teaching load does not go down as research expectations go up. But the bigger problem is that over the last decade, service expectations have gone up more dramatically.  The "extra" stuff that professors do - advise student, provide promotional copy for the website, interact with industry, give presentations at high schools, advise clubs, mentor student research projects, write up endless assessment reports for the administration - that stuff has exploded. One reason is that there are few fulltime faculty left - most teaching is now done by adjuncts who do not do service work.  So the result is, I work 7 days a week during the semesters. My summer luxury is, gasp, not working on weekends.  Most of my summer is consumed with  publishing, chasing grants, and hours doing end of year assessment reports. Welcome to the real work of academia.

Hardigree's statement that higher education is "a service industry" is the stupidest thing I hear today.) But we know that online, remote education is at best adequate, and that in-person instruction (and mentoring, etc.) is a superior mode of learning. Remote education is little more than glorified auto-didacticism. Why have teachers at all? Give the students library access and let 'em go.

"Another kind of opening is offered by the subway’s many air vents, used instead of air-conditioning"

I hate to be this guy, but it is to an important point: The air vents were for induction, not as a replacement for air conditioning. The engineering idea was that rushing trains would pull fresh air through one grate and expel it from another. This was to save from acquiring land and building large fan structures like those used on the vehicle tunnels connecting Manhattan to everywhere.  

The subway engineers back then figured that the weather assumptions they made in the late 1800s-early 1900s would not change and 100 years from the opening of the system, contemporary engineers would solve problems with novel solutions. The MTA started the homework way too late and is now on the backfoot of Mother Nature.

comments.name: William
comments.body:
Put all the trains above ground and call it a day. The city already has all the built-in drainage it needs: it's called the subway system. That's the function it's already performing anyway, and from the photos and videos I see here, it's doing a great job. 

The problem is that you have millions of people trying to commute through a drainage system. Not a great way to commute -- ask any New Yorker.

So instead of "fixing" subway drainage for multi-billions of dollars over a span of decades, FACE REALITY (I know, it's hard) and move the entire transit system above ground, with rails on the streets and additional elevated. A lot cheaper and more effective than trying to figure out how to renovate something underground when underground is so impossibly complicated with tunnels and sewage pipes and water supply and electrical cables and Jimmy Hoffa and Vince Mangano and god knows who else. You never know what you'll find -- better to not even look.

Yes, you'd have to virtually eliminate almost all motor vehicles from large sections of the city, especially Manhattan and the Bronx, but that could be a good thing for the air quality and for making the new above-ground trains pay for themselves. New York is going to be flooded more and more, and either you have to raise everything higher or you have to move the city itself away from the ocean and rivers. 

Bring the trains above ground and let the tunnels drain all the water that's going to keep coming and coming and coming.

comments.name: justgimmesometruth
comments.body:
I live in Bangkok, a city of population comparable to that of NYC, with a beautiful modern metro system. However, the NYC system does carry more passengers daily, has somewhat more track-miles, and has about twice as many stations.

The NYC system is 120 years old and clearly falling apart. The band-aids are no longer working well. So, why can't one of the wealthiest cities in the world begin building a new system?

There are many reasons, but an obvious one is construction cost. In Bangkok, the cost of construction of an underground metro is US$150–350 million/km while in New York City it is US$1.5–2.5+ billion/km.

In Thailand, the Thai government provides a lot of support to building new lines and stations. In the US, public transport is simply not a national priority.

Also, many (not all) of the Thai lines are elevated, avoiding flooding problems. Stations, elevated or underground, have EXACTLY two entrances. Fare-beating doesn't happen here.

The Skytrain station is just outside the entrance to my condo. I never rush to catch a train and I never stress if I arrive when a train is leaving. The next train will arrive within 3 minutes.

NYC, and the US in general, could do a lot better... then again, we do have wars to fight.

comments.body: Just like Sonia Bordlies says, this is family here. I wouldn’t trade my pool for nothing. I see my summer high being out at my grandparents' farm, where we have gone for years. My summer never feels like summer until I'm out there four-wheeling and spending time with family, and no money can buy that feeling away. When I'm sitting on the revving engine, going around the farm I have memorized since I was 6, it just feels like I'm free. Although not everyone has a farm or a pricey camp that they go to, I believe that everyone has a place during summer that makes them feel free, and that summer is truly here.

comments.name: Isla G
comments.body: Summer is not my favorite season by any means. It’s hot, sticky, and is filled with constant long days of life guarding at my local public pool. The worst part about working at the pool is there is never any good time to sit back and enjoy a good bite to eat, the only thing I can count on is the complementary individual cups of ice cream, just like Melissa Kirsch used to enjoy at camp. What really tastes like summer to me though is the sweet squeakers dessert at the state fair. As I bite into the funnel cake battered cheese curd, with whipped cream, and the brightest tasting strawberry jam drizzled on top, I reminisce about the start of summer. The early June days where I look forward to the spontaneous drives, early sunrise walks, and least expecting of all, getting to talk with the pool rats that make my seasonal job stop feeling like a chore, and instead a home.

comments.name: Micah
comments.body: As Elizabeth Passerella writes in this excerpt “... summer is to be endured, rather than enjoyed.” In the same way, my summer was more one of enduring. I spent it working, cleaning, and progressing my research project. As much as I love these tasks, they can be trivial. There were many days where I worked 12 hours in a row and while the work wasn’t hard, it was almost painful to sit through; Task after task, conversation after conversation, problem after problem. In addition to working, I spent some of my summer time cleaning. I cleaned my grandparent’s house biweekly, only about an hour at a time, but only to hear the same comments about things that my grandparents thought were “new.” The most strenuous thing I did this summer was start and work on my research project, many late nights and one too many math theory papers read, but I chose to endure it.

comments.name: Leah
comments.body: Like Elizabeth Passarella writes in “It’s okay to hate Summer” summer is more to be endured than enjoyed. I don’t enjoy the lack of schedule, the bugs, and the excessive heat. Therefore, I believe that the best season comes right after summer. I think that everything about fall is just much more enjoyable such as the leaves changing, getting to wear longer clothing, and getting to drink a pumpkin chai. Summer definitely has its moments, like when I get to see my friends more and not having to wake up early, but I enjoy being able to be in a scheduled routine instead.

comments.name: Khalid
comments.body: I’ve never gotten the hype around summer. The bugs, heat, and body odor of others all seem to get on my nerves. Just as Elizabeth Passarella states her stress level rises with a lack of routine, mine too rises along with the heat of summer. My family seems to have different opinions about summer though. They love the outdoors and whenever we have an outing, I always try to warn them about the dangers of summer. I mention ticks, bug bites, and dehydration, yet none of these concerns even phase them! In the end I always end up getting dragged along with them, much to my despair.

articles.title: How Was Your Summer?
articles.summary: What were the highs and lows of the season for you?

comments.name: Kathy
comments.body: Around the world, men are supposed to be both much bigger and stronger than women, and simultaneously unable to control themselves around us. Who else wants to have their cake and eat it too? Stop oppressing us, men, and your lives will improve dramatically.

comments.name: Krunal
comments.body: So let me understand this: they asked whether an accommodation could be made because their monks follow an extremely strict religious vow of celibacy, the organization agreed, and somehow you’ve turned that into “women are inferior”? Who exactly appointed you the judge of which religious practices are acceptable? You call yourself liberal while demanding that someone else’s faith conform to your beliefs. Religious tolerance apparently only counts when you personally approve of the religion.

comments.name: Pascale Luse
comments.body: Those Hindu visitors have acted against the basic HUMAN RIGHTS of french workers by asking women to be excluded. Not only the acceptance of this repugnant condition for the Eiffel Tower visit should have been refused but this group of weirdos should have been immediately expelled from France for asking such a condition!

comments.name: Frederic Mokren
comments.body:
Every time I think we are making progress in the world we get a story like this. I can, unfortunately, ignore the backwards thinking of the Hindu religious group, but why in 2026 do people still go along with this kind of thinking? 

Who is saying to themselves, "This seems like a reasonable request," and then actually following through on this? I'm gobsmacked. 

Men like to complain, "but not all men." It really only takes one man who still thinks like it's 1855 and other men to follow along.

comments.name: Noor Jahan
comments.body: Unbelievable! Who made the decision to change the staffing at the Eiffel tower for one group of visitors? Perhaps the BAPS monks need to learn how to control their desires and not look at females as sexual objects. Why is it the responsibility of women and girls to cover their hair or wear dresses (no trousers) or follow some other restriction dictated by the men in their respective religions so as not to "tempt" the men and boys? Asking females to hide themselves is a way to control them and exert power over them. Men like the BAPS monks need to examine their own weaknesses and insecurities, and not use religion to oppress females.

comments.name: Equilibrium
comments.body:
This is why I have massive issues with all faiths that exhibit fundamentalism and extreme views. 

This is absolutely outrageous. it says in the story that the monks can' speak or touch women. OK notify staff, so they respect that and the monks can avoid interacting with the women. Forcing the women to be discriminated against because of the monks restrictions is absurd.

All these faiths that have so much fear of women, this one in the article, many sects of Christianity, Catholicism, Islam, Judaism, buddhism and on and on and on. 

Religion has caused so much discrimination and suffering in the world, and yes some good, but it is clearly in the minority, and almost always the women doing it. Not the men.

Practice your faith in your own sphere and leave the rest of ALONE.

Truth be told men are terrified of women in these religions and they know that the women would be wiser, more humane, more accepting, and more decent.

comments.name: Jen R
comments.body:
Just because I'm vegetarian doesn't mean that restaurants are going to throw out all the meat dishes when I want to go there.

If you're a monk and you have forsaken all the world's temptations then that includes being tested. You should maintain equanimity in front of women, hamburgers, Fox News.

 It's not impressive to be a monk if inside your ashram you're all the time. If you want to come out into the world to build a temple, that is where you are tested to show. If you truly are renouncing earthly desires. If you can't resist temptation when it's right in front of you then think of a different career.

comments.name: ItCouldBeWorse
comments.body: How did the BAPS members get to Paris?  Private busing?  Surely not by public transportation.

articles.title: Eiffel Tower Workers Strike, Saying Women Were Excluded From Hindu Group’s Visit
articles.summary: The tower was closed on Monday, after the workers’ union said female staff members had been asked to leave their stations for a visit from a group known as BAPS.

comments.name: Demosthenes
comments.body: Private street, private beach. Private calamity? Lucky for the residents who can afford to fix it.

comments.name: loudfun
comments.body: is that really a bright green grass lawn across the street from Cage's house?  Don't look far for one of the culprits.

comments.name: E Plurbis Unum
comments.body:
Building on a slope or shoreline in California requires consideration of substrate.

This seems to work on the Amalfi Coast.

Build a house on an overlook in Malibu and you better plan on relocating when the Pacific repossesses the property.

Sorry, Mr Cage.  But maybe there is a movie in this.

comments.name: Julie Tea
comments.body: This why the ocean front shouldn’t be in private hands. There’s a set back in Canada from the actual sea. It should be bigger than it is but it prevents truly ridiculous building such as seen in the photos here.

comments.name: Upsidedown1
comments.body: Bad investment. It should be obvious.

comments.name: CC
comments.body:
I feel bad for him and everyone else who has an unexpected disaster threaten their home.

When the movie comes out, I know he will triumph, and it will be every bit as ridiculous as the inciting event.

comments.name: Hello there
comments.body: Calling all commenters here, may we please have a moratorium on the use of the phrase "Mother Nature"? It's a tad old. Meanwhile, good luck to Mr. Cage and neighbors.

comments.name: Michael D
comments.body: Obviously it collapsed beneath the unbearable weight of his massive talent.

comments.name: Jason
comments.body: This is so much whining. If government support were enough, China would not have a property crisis. Each of these successes came from decades long bets. Europe spent its years handicapping its industries with taxes on climate change. Where has that money gone? The US grew rich, but with financialization, the money sits in funds and stocks. Profits are all that matter.

comments.name: individual 1
comments.body: The United States should have implemented trade policies penalizing any nation—China or otherwise—maintaining a surplus with the country centuries ago. A fundamental principle of trade should be that the U.S. receives equal value for each dollar exchanged, with no nation permitted to sustain a deficit. This imbalance reflects a failure by U.S. policymakers and those in positions of authority to fulfill their responsibilities in safeguarding national economic interests.

comments.name: Robert R
comments.body: Our government tariffs and trade policies opened the door for China. Now the administration is complaining? Look in the mirror.

articles.title: China’s Surging Exports Loom Over Trump’s Talks With Xi
articles.summary: China’s exports grew by a quarter in the month of August, weeks before its leader, Xi Jinping, is set to meet with President Trump in Washington.

comments.name: K
comments.body: After Dexa scans in my early 40's (done due to family history) indicated low bone density my doctor told me I needed daily jumping exercises. She said I needed the impact from jumping and that resistance alone would not be enough. A second doctor repeated this. So I jumped. A lot. And broke an ankle. Not from a fall, but from repeated stress to the bone. I don't think anyone really knows how to handle low bone density in non-menopausal women. I have no idea now how I am supposed to manage this diagnosis.

comments.name: Linda Brown
comments.body: My doctor recommended one almost 10 years ago, so I made an appointment with a speciliast. It revealed I had severe  osteoporosis. We discussed options for medication and agreed on the  one with the fewest risks. My insurance didn't cover it, so I started walking more, using resistance band exercises in imititation of our astronauts, and increasing my calcium supplements in the dosage  prescribed by my GP.  I don't know what the future holds, but I haven't broken anything so far despite being 74 and falling more often.

comments.name: Angie
comments.body: I had a DEXA scan at 43 which showed osteopenia. When I had a second one this year at 47 it showed obvious osteoporosis. I have had 2 hip fractures, including a replacement, and a foot fracture. Do it now if you can so you can correct it. Hip fractures from falling hurt more than I can even explain.

comments.name: Kathleen Clarke
comments.body: There is no mention in this piece that  a referral to a PT who specializes in the management of osteoporosis.  Posture can change dramatically  and a solid fall prevention program can prevent fracture

comments.name: IB
comments.body: At 56, 2 years post-menopausal, I read in the local paper that women with a family history of osteoporosis should be screened at 50.  I was stunned to discover that I was definitively osteoporotic.  If I'd waited till 65, my bones would have been powder - or I would have been diagnosed after a fracture before then.  Once again, medical standards are inconsistent and consistently fail women.

comments.name: Maureen
comments.body: I am 56 and had my 1st DEXA scan last year.  It showed I am on the edge of osteopenia.  For many reasons, I cannot take HRT, so I started a program called ONERO.  I recommend any woman at risk to find an ONERO program near you.  It is tailored for us and results have shown it can reverse signs of osteopenia and osteoporosis and increase bone health.

comments.name: Ophelia
comments.body:
I got an executive physical with DEXA scan in my early 40s that showed strong bone density, good levels of Vitamin D, and a solid muscle mass baseline. This information made me feel confident that my exercise and dietary habits are working well and motivated to keep them up; I'll get another scan in about a decade as my hormones shift to check for changes. 

A friend of mine also got the scan and found osteopenia, so she is starting more rigorous resistance training and may be faster to pursue estrogen or other treatment. I do think a scan at the start of perimenopause is a valuable baseline that can give women the opportunity to change behaviors or pursue treatment before its too late.

comments.name: lynn
comments.body: I'm 62. Last year I slipped on ice and broke my right wrist. My PCP sent me for the scan and it shows osteopenia on my hip, arm and spine. I have been fairly active for decades but mostly cardio. Now I took up weight training 3-4 times per week. Will get another scan next year. What frustrates me is that I asked for DEXA scan 7 years ago while I was going thru menopause but the provider who was seeing me at the time refused my request. Her reason: "I'm practicing evidence medicine. there is no obvious risk factor for you at this time. ". I had to have a broken wrist to get the scan. I'm furious!

articles.title: When Do Women Really Need a Bone Scan?
articles.summary: Some doctors and influencers say women shouldn’t wait until their 60s for a DEXA scan. Here’s what to consider before getting one.

comments.name: DAK
comments.body: i always wandered what the house in hillsdale on nobletown rd was in a former life. it was a church. Thanks nyt for that info. i think the house is being renovated now. my husband always said, he’d love to live near a cemetery because he wouldn’t have to worry about noisy neighbors or unkempt properties.

comments.name: Timo
comments.body: There's a kind of timelessness I experience in cemeteries: a sense of being absolutely present, consciously connected to the past and, as a result, envisioning the future. I find it very grounding; the triviality of most things becomes apparent, and the relative importance of the eternal fundamentals—love, security, the pleasure of the senses, imagination, intellect—become that much clearer.

comments.name: Rick Sacks.
comments.body: Old cemeteries, like old stone walls, mark a time we cannot return to. I love roaming through forests or the outskirts of towns and finding this remnants of  'back then'. I will be donating my body to a medical school.

comments.name: chris
comments.body: In the picture gallery for the first house it says that the deed requires the cemetery to be moved.  More explanation seems necessary.

comments.name: anonymous
comments.body:
Just saying:
Some would find just treading on the ground of buried of dear ones more than mildly offensive, highly disrespectful. Consider that decay and overgrowth are natural and may have been intentional and desired

comments.name: Gert
comments.body: Had I to do it over, I would've looked for a house in or really close to a cemetery. You couldn't ask for better neighbors.  They're all dead.

comments.name: OBatl
comments.body: That Queens house and graveyard! Love that. We used to live across the street from a lesser known cemetery in New Orleans where the cemetery occupied two full city blocks. We loved the quietude as those neighbors were our best behaved. Our block with only 5 actual houses turned out to be both modest and desirable for its peacefulness. The nightly lock up of the cemetery by Catholic Cemeteries was key to this peace which kept shenanigans from taking place in the walled/high-fenced cemetery at night. I'd live there again in a minute and the cemetery was interesting and orderly by day for a stroll.

comments.name: Anonymous
comments.body: In late fall of 1969 my Father sent a letter to me with an article from the front page of the "St. Louis Globe-Democrat." The brother of my girlfriend at the time had been killed. He was a grave digger at the time, and I had just seen him a few weeks before when I traveled back to St. Louis from Columbia where I was a freshman at the University of Missouri. This article is poignant for me because the last time I ever saw him when we said "goodbye," I said, "Don't get buried in your work." His younger sister, my girlfriend, and her parents were of course devastated by the loss. When I saw them again at Christmas her parents just seemed hollow and their home vacant of all feeling. My girlfriend's brother was a brilliant, but eccentric guy. He scored 800 on the SAT math and verbal,but when he went to Washington University he spent all his time golfing in nearby Forest Park.The dean called his parents and said that though he was enrolled, no professor had ever seen him.So much for "WashU." One night he was riding with friends in an open convertible and some toughs threw a hamburger bun into the car. His friends followed the guys to their home and one of the bun throwers yanked him out of the car and killed him.I've always regretted my pun.Older now I think more about how I say goodbye to people.Puns and gallows humor were common in the hospitals where I spent most of career.Tense situations are often made less stressful,but I've mostly avoided them since my cemetery one long ago.

articles.title: For People Who Live in Cemeteries, the Scariest Thing May Be the Puns
articles.summary: Occupants of “houses to die for” say the advantages go beyond quiet neighbors.

comments.name: Charlie
comments.body:
---
Nice to see Jesse Green’s byline.

First saw the original Sullivan Street production wa-a-a-ay back in ’62, when it was a relative newcomer to off-B’way.  I do recall that the talented Carole Demas was playing the girl at that point.

Have acted in two productions of THE FANTASTICKS (perhaps the most often mis-spelled title of all musicals) – once as The Mute and once as El Gallo.

And I directed an English-language production in Japan, changing one of the dads into a mom – mainly because of a limited talented pool available to choose from.  (This gender-reversal was sacrilegious at the time!)

A couple of years later a Broadway-sized touring production of THE FANTASTICKS played a big professional theater in Tokyo – with Mr. Jones as Henry and Mr. Schmidt behind the piano.  I had the opportunity after the performance to tell each of them of my long and undying devotion to their musical gem.

And Robert Goulet (as El Gallo) led a large touring production -- featuring a 17-member cast -- that played at Wolf Trap in suburban DC back in 1990.

So: an inflated production of THE FANTASTICKS is not unprecedented.

P.S. This article’s reader comments confirm that this musical’s title is probably the most frequently mis-spelled in the history of American theater!
---

comments.name: JeanieDiva
comments.body: I join with all those, particularly here in NYC, who support any expression of gay individuals that allows them to be seen for who they are, without condemnation. I have worked with theater performers here since 1980, and I don't think this new version is fair to the older one. I know, it happens all the time as in the recent "Cats: The Jellical Ball" but if you change so much of a classic, it's really a new show. Same thing that happens in opera. Is Don Giovanni with the Don as a mafia capo still Don Giovanni? Hm.......we'll see how it goes.

comments.name: george
comments.body: SOOOO glad to see anything written by Jesse Green!  Thank you.

comments.name: Andrew
comments.body: If the songs are excellent - and the orchestrations are not completely off the rails - I never cared who was singing to whom or why. Most opera storylines are cartoonish nonsense but the music endures.

comments.name: Ray
comments.body: I am less disturbed by making the lovers two gay men than Broadway “supersizing” the darn near perfect orchestrations for two pianos and harp, especially the musical’s stirring overture. The show’s charm is its simplicity and intimacy, not always Broadway’s strong suit.

comments.name: CA English Teacher
comments.body:
I've played Matt once and directed The Fantasticks twice, once for a university production and once for a professional touring show. 

I agree with those who question the need for this production . . . and those who question its potential success in today's very challenging market. I have a feeling it will go the way of Cats: The Jellicle Ball. 

One other thought: If The Fantasticks has been gay all along because of all the gay actors, writers, directors, costumers, designers, and Schmidt himself, then EVERY musical has been gay all along(!).

comments.name: tyrdofwaitin
comments.body: I saw the original in the 60s after coming out, but before Stonewall. Frankly, I fell asleep a couple times; I wasn't into straight romances at the time. Now, I would love seeing young love between boys ---as I was 60 years ago. This time, it's unlikely I will fall asleep.

comments.name: ALP
comments.body: Maxim Chlumecky, is so insanely talented!  I am so very excited to have the opportunity to see him perform on Broadway in this beautiful show.

articles.title: How Luisa Became Lewis in the World’s Longest-Running Musical
articles.summary: “The Fantasticks” ran for decades in Greenwich Village. Now, in time for its Broadway debut, it gets a gender makeover.

comments.name: Not a sweetie
comments.body:
We own property north of Lahaina that was not affected by the fire but have friends who were. It is hard for people not from Maui to understand the devastation, both physical and mental, that overtook Lahaina in a matter of hours. 

What this article ignores is the well-meaning attempts to preserve the old ways and beauty by laws and bureaucracy that made new construction both more costly and exceedingly slow. Instead of dealing with growth, Maui tried to prevent it. Those who could afford the spiraling costs stayed. Others left. The joke became that Las Vegas was the 8th Hawaiian Island because of so many service workers fleeing there. Sadly, little has been done to create more affordable, buildable land, to reduce permitting times, and to deal with the upside-down economics of Maui. Maui Mayor, Bessin, is championing a massive reduction of short-term rentals that panders to locals, but actually exacerbates the housing problem,

Until Hawaii's politicians come to terms with basic economics, the state's problems, and Maui's. will not improve.

comments.name: Sharkbetty Crips
comments.body: Fire is one of the things that was largely unheard of when I moved here 37 years  ago. Same for hurricanes (rare) and thunderstorms (rare). The biggest impact of climate change for me is the degradation of the trade winds. Windless days are more frequent and it’s nearly unbearable. These conditions also create mold bombs. All your fabric, Leather and cardboard gets covered in green mold slime. Ruined. Nobody had air conditioners when I moved here because the trades were reliable. Thats no longer true. In fact, I’m going to buy an air conditioner today, it’s been just miserable this summer.

comments.name: Drippy CC
comments.body:
Hopefully, locals and Native Hawaiians recognize that Hawaii now operates within a global marketplace. The Hawaiian and Polynesian diaspora has been underway for decades, and attempting to stop economic migration through ever-greater barriers will not reverse it. That brings me to my larger point: what I see as “radical empathy” is increasingly overriding economic pragmatism.

I want the free market to function so the economy can grow. I don’t support the immigration or social policies of parties such as Germany’s AfD, but I’m frustrated that much of the American left has moved away from the market-oriented economic policies once embraced by mainstream Democrats.

What happened to politicians who competed for the moderate middle? While the media, political activists, and educated elites fight endless culture wars, our governing institutions have become increasingly incapable of compromise. If elected officials cannot debate, negotiate, and pass meaningful legislation, the country stagnates.

Obama’s 2008 campaign famously promised “CHANGE,” yet nearly two decades later, many Americans still feel our political system has delivered remarkably little structural change. Meanwhile, cultural attitudes have shifted dramatically. Issues once well outside mainstream political debate are now treated as central priorities. To me, that reflects a larger problem: empathy, when elevated above economics, democratic consensus, and practical governance, can become counterproductive.

comments.name: Publius
comments.body: "One politician estimated that it could take up to a decade or more before the town is fully rebuilt."  As with New Orleans after Katrina, there is no money to rebuild an American city destroyed by disaster, but plenty for endless wars and billionaire tax cuts.

comments.name: Gramie 2RMJ
comments.body: What was lost in Lahaina was not the tourist - not the draw of beauty - not the “what cold have been” - not just the lives - but the livelihood. The struggle to survive on native land will be lost forever. in this area of Maui. While the investors from both mainland and abroad will have their way with the rebuild  - the people, the pets, the flora and fauna the heartbeat of Lahaina will never live the life they had. Oh, the land and the sea, the views attempts to revive are there. The hope of home, the hope of hope went up in flames for those who called their paradise their heart, their home. If ever there was a reason for federal significant intervention - Lahaina was the victim to support.

comments.name: UKgirl
comments.body:
I will never understand how considering the many zillionaires that have homes on Maui cannot help out the Lahaina community. 

Surely they  could come together and build homes and give back to the beautiful people of Lahaina, while barely making a dent in their net worth? They could change lives yet they do nothing. 
What happened to the millions Bezos was supposed to have donated and Oprah, who has had a home on Maui for decades, did her contributions end? It’s a disgrace.
My heart is with you Lahaina .

comments.name: t.bruch
comments.body: no mention of the 160 manufactured homes shipped to maui to help families that lost there homes

articles.title: ‘We’re Going to Bring It Back to Life’: The Long Road to Reviving Lahaina
articles.summary: Hawaii’s housing crisis was at a breaking point even before the fire. Since then, displaced families have struggled to rebuild their lives.

comments.name: c
comments.body: If I remember my high school French, doesn’t “fou” also mean crazy?

comments.name: Rita
comments.body: So how does this compare with the Asterix the Gaul theme park?

comments.name: Tony
comments.body:
Who needs this? France is so incredibly beautiful  I wouldn't waste a minute while in France at any "theme" park. 

From my experience, the French love spending their holidays visiting the countryside, the museums, the villages and enjoying the cuisine.

I'll pass...

comments.name: Jin Defang
comments.body: enjoy it, but also see sites like Chateau Coucy ---almost deserted when I went there---to get a fuller picture of French history. In the case of Coucy, just a part of it, of course.

comments.name: xoxo
comments.body: For accuracy: The Disney Company indeed has a site near Paris that they operate and partially own, sometimes referred to by its actual name, Disneyland Paris...but Disneyland is a theme park in California and it does not have any sites near Paris!

comments.name: Alexander
comments.body: People can have pride in their country.  Despite the many terrible things that many European countries did during colonialism, they are the prime destinations for refugees in the Middle East and Africa.  And as a Floridian, I see people all the time who have migrated to my state who have pride in where they are from without making some huge political case about it.  I don’t assume that a person with a Cuban flag dangling from their mirror is a hardcore marxist-leninist.

comments.name: Sam M
comments.body:
Entertainment should not be a substitute for robust education in civics and history. When such knowledge gaps exist people simply believe what they hear, a vulnerability exploited by ideologues on all sides. 

If citizens are susceptible to fascist propaganda from a theme park, this must be resolved in the classroom, not by building a leftist theme park across the street.

comments.name: KM
comments.body: Nothing outrages the left like their narrative being challenged. And for those whining about inaccuracies, leftist revisionist history is just as warped and selective, so they have no stones to throw.

articles.title: The Theme Park at the Heart of France’s Culture War
articles.byline: Catherine Porter, Giulia Imbert and William Daniels
articles.summary: The Puy du Fou is one of France’s most visited theme parks. Its founder says it gives the French a “founding narrative,” but critics say it peddles “far-right propaganda.”

comments.name: Karen Leeds
comments.body:
To the friend of the woman with the nanny. Not your monkey, not your circus. I was managing caregivers for my mother and one would consistently be late. She was being paid by the hour and although late, she would always leave on time but still charge my mom for the whole shift. It drove my mom - who was a depression baby and very frugal - nuts.  One day my mother asked her why she was always late. Alandra simply denied it and yelled at my 95 year old mom for picking on her. I fired her. 

To the weed smoker’s neighbor. If it’s legal, theres not much you can do about it but I was curious how many minutes a day does this guy actually smoke pot? And unless the smoke lingers like a low hanging cloud, it’s not permanently invading the air you breathe. But if you really hate it, say something. Your neighbor is not likely to stop but at least he’ll know he’s driving you crazy.

comments.name: albert
comments.body: After 10 years, there is almost no chance for recocilation.  This is a lesson for everyone to keep their mouth shut.  There is no reason to tell others about the personal matters of others.

comments.name: globe
comments.body: I do not understand why the ex husband having an illness would be the catalyst to telling a family “secret.”  I feel the estrangement from mother was more complex than presented. Cutting off all contact did nothing toward resolution or acceptance of the injured party.

comments.name: SouthernHope
comments.body: Here's a genuine question for the letter writer: *Why* did you believe that your former husband needed to know about your child's gender transition. That is, what was it about that information that you felt it was necessary for him to know before he passed away? My guess is that it was done for attention on your part and my guess is that your child realized that and just said, "I am done."

comments.name: Matt
comments.body:
Is there a paragraph or something missing from LW1? 

What part of "she told me I was free to talk about it" is ambiguous?

Listen, if I had an estranged child, I would confess to being the unibomber if it would help, but the mother is either omitting some pertinent details or has done absolutely nothing wrong.

comments.name: P.
comments.body:
Life is ‘funny’, isn’t it?

Oof, I’d choose a different word than ‘funny’.

comments.name: Love4Cats
comments.body: Why do people, presumably not family or friends who would already know, care what day a child is born? Seems odd.

comments.name: Fomo brood

comments.name: James Schumaker
comments.body:
Nuclear power is inherently dangerous as long as there is no place to store spent fuel safely. Current dry cask storage on-site works for a century or so, but it is vulnerable in the event of war, terrorist attack, or radiation leaks. The storage method seems safe, but is good only for about 100 years at best. We need safe storage, secure from all hazards, for thousands of years.

That's one reason why renewable sources of energy, such as solar and wind, are much safer and cheaper in the long run than nuclear. Characteristically, the Trump administration is hell-bent on eliminating subsidies for renewable energy, while maintaining them for nuclear. In a rational world, it should be the other way around.

Missing in this article, this nuclear plant sits atop or near 4 earthquake fault lines. It has been retrofitted to withstand a 7.5 quake, but, California has had more than their share of quakes at or above that strength.
I started college there in very nearby San Luis Obispo in 1987. While showering in an interior bathroom, no windows and the door closed, I heard the very loud sirens warning there was a problem at the power plant. Got out of the shower and did what I was supposed to do, shove towels against the bottom of the door and windows. It was later determined it was a human error. But, after Three Mile Island, frightening.

comments.name: John Dunlap
comments.body: Think of our energy resources (i.e., solar, wind, geothermal, tidal, geothermal, batteries storage, nuclear, and if need be a bit of gas) as a diversified portfolio similar to how people invest for retirement.  Generally, you want to have a mix - a diversified portfolio to reduce risk.  For this reason, I reluctantly support Diablo Canyon since the facility already exists and it can help provide electricity diversification especially when the sun sets.  That said, I do think solar plus battery tech have the potential to provide a significant portion of our electrify needs at substantially less cost than other conventional options not to mention the significant environmental benefits of solar as compared to carbon-based oil or coal.  So simply put, think of your energy needs as a diversified portfolio, weigh your options, and if the costs/environmental benefits are advantageous, skew the state's energy portfolio and production toward cheaper solar and wind, with backup options.

comments.name: Bruce Higgins
comments.body:
The latest front on the nuclear power issue is not massive nuclear plants to power AI Data Centers, it is Microreactors at military bases.   General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems was recently tapped as one of five initial vendors for the Janus Program — the Army’s $2.2 billion effort to deploy commercial microreactors within the next two years, on Army bases around the nation.  

The military is trying to protect itself from the prospect of a massive Grid Failure in the US leaving the military both blind and unable to respond to a threat.

No mention so far about what is to be done with the high level nuclear waste produced by the Army's on base microreactors.  There is currently no national repository for high level nuclear waste.  The waste from commercial reactors is currently stored on site at the power plant and is likely to be there for many decades.  One would assume the same would apply to military reactor waste.

The other branches of the military are also going to want their own reactors, they can't have the Army showing them up.  So we will likely have reactor envy, and microreactors sprouting up where ever there is a major military base.

There are hundreds of unanswered questions:  Do local authorities have the power to forbid the installation of a nuclear reactor on a military base in their state, county, city?  What happens when there is an emergency at the reactor, who responds, who is notified, what about the public right to know?   On and On. . .

comments.name: Dave
comments.body:
Headline says California is an environmental bastion. 
Therefore it should warm to nuclear energy instead of shunning it. Nuclear power is virtually free of carbon dioxide emissions. Even taking into account co2 emissions from the cement used to make the power plants, nuclear power is less co2 producing that solar power including the emissions from producing the panels. 
Also nuclear power results about the same number of deaths per unit of energy generated as solar or wind. Almost all deaths in nuclear, solar, and wind come from installations and operations. 
I once thought nuclear power plants shouldn’t be built, but only because of the waste disposal problem. But more than 25 years ago I realized that was just a red herring. The plans to permanently store nuclear waste have been thwarted by scare mongers. However, we use the next best option is on site storage. The amount of waste seems large based upon weight but the volume isn’t large. 
I’ve been an environmental advocate since the 70s, and I am very dismayed (really I’m angry) with so many environmental organizations for working to stop nuclear power. Finally some are changing. If we had built more nuclear power plants, we would not have any coal or gas powered power plants now and we could have eliminated them 20 years ago or more.

It also incurs significant traffic from 101 and 280 off-ramps and the next northern 101 on-ramp. Traffic chaos regularly.
It’s wildly frustrating to be behind a single Zoox, never mind two or three, that stops and waits a count of 5 before proceeding through a 4-way stop, throwing the smooth flow of heavy traffic into a cluster… .
But, it’s also fascinating to watch how each model learns and adapts. R.I.P. Cruise. Waymo has gotten appropriately aggressive with those off-ramp drivers who don’t wait their turn at 4-ways. Zoox still putters along without seeming to adapt at all, except maybe stopping only 3 seconds at 4-way stops. Is this a conscious strategy against risk or does it reflect the quality of their engineering teams?

comments.name: CPL593H
comments.body:
The U.S. government erred from the start in treating this and the whole A.I. copyright fiasco as a dispute to be litigated in civil court when they should have treated it as what it is: a conspiracy to commit widespread copyright infringement. And yes, the venture capital investors are a party to that conspiracy. 

Copyright law exists to facilitate parties that, at least on some level, want or need to do business with each other. But there is nothing in copyright law that says that you have to make a deal with someone when you don't want to, or that if someone steals enough stuff from enough people and turns around and sells it that it magically becomes just a business dispute. 

If a real estate agent or short term rental company shows up and says that they want to make money renting your home and you refuse and one day when you are at work they go like gangsters and do it anyway and pocket the money just as they said they would, that agent or company has committed a crime by exploiting a property to which they have no title or contractual right and they are going to jail and/or paying serious criminal penalties. For some reason the U.S. government has basically decided that as long as people are doing this as part of a company with millions/billions in investment, well, hey, it's a business dispute. Sorry you lost your house. Maybe you should make a deal...

And then when enough deals are made—all of them bad—the gangsters have officially taken over the industry.
