comments.name: dan100"
comments.body:
You can win a chess tournament if you use a computer with advanced chess playing software.
This is a solution if the goal is to win at all cost, including eliminating the need for human's input.

Similarly, you can create tons of music with the AI plegerizing machines, requiring minimal input from a human. 

So why bother to learn how to play an instrument or learn to think about planning strategy? AI can do the job. 

Sarcasm aside, I am on the side of humanity. I think of art as an extension of human expression, much of it tied to to our cultures and experiences. Who needs millons of versions of say country western, rap or hundreds of Beethoven's style (symphony #10?).

There is a lot of concern regarding AI replacing people's jobs. AI music generation is done inside a digital machine. No need for microphones or recording equipment, or the humans "making the sounds". AI music  is already causing pain and layoffs to artists. 

I am on the side of humanity. I hope we win!

comments.name: Charles
comments.body:
Some 25 years ago now, we were attended a Disney On Ice performance and drove by picketers at the entrance to the parking lot with signs indicating Disney was unfair to musicians. When I got home, I investigated. It turns out it was the musician's union and that Disney had done away with live musicians in favor of recorded music. Upon reflection, it appeared true as there was only a live percussionist adding "effects" to what was a prerecorded soundtrack. This was Windows 95 times and long before AI..

Now, unfortunately, we live in a world of music performed by artists, many of whom, don't read music nor have mastered the craft of any instrument. This includes to instrument of their own vocals as autotune and other augmentation has proliferated. This is the world of "machine" music. Creative? Of course. Musicianship? Hardly.

Now, enter AI. Now its "fake musicianship" on steroids. While, I suppose, there is nothing wrong with its being entertaining, however, when we come to complain about value, quality, and "shrinkflation" in America, the world of music is exhibit #1.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body:
This article doesn't say enough about what Suno and their ilk are doing to already exploitative music streaming services. They are increasingly filling up with "artists" releasing a new album of 10-14 3:00 +/- 0:10 length songs every week, usually with twee lowercase song titles and slop album art. If you ever have the misfortune of "the algorithm" playing even one of these songs, you will soon get flooded with a torrent of similar garbage.

Time to retreat to Bandcamp, SoundCloud and the like, I suppose. Unfortunately, fraudsters are also taking of advantage of what must be huge increases in "new content" uploaded to these platforms to engage in more old-fashioned fraud like hijacking artist pages by releasing tracks under the same name, or outright claiming other artists' work as their own as minimal remixes. I've even seen newly-registered accounts backdating albums with "AI art" that couldn't possibly have been generated a decade ago.

The end result is real human artists are going to be crowded out, even more so than when streaming services became so consolidated. Established musicians may be fine, but what about new entrants without shiny record deals, and for how much longer?

comments.name: Uncle Leo
comments.body:
One huge piece of the "puzzle", as it were, that most articles - including this one - seem to gloss over, or miss completely, is that from a musician's perspective, songwriting, arranging, production and all the activities associated with creating a piece of music are intensely personal, creative endeavors.  There is absolutely no way in heaven, hell or earth that can change that.

The business part of it is a different animal.  All products like SUNO do (I tried it out of curiosity and, well, let's just say I don't use it any more) is to automate the generation and regurgitation of ideas that other people have used - but blindly.  It's like a jazz musician playing solos based entirely on rules that specify which scales go over which chords.  As a result, they DO produce slop.  Unfortunately, this works very well in our current world of mediocrity where quantity reigns over quality.

Can you just imagine Aja being produced using SUNO?  Please!!

Think of one person's lifetime of experiences responding, reacting, feeling and suffering; through injuries, loss of loved ones; broken relationships, loss of a job, a home, a community; loss of identity. Think of the music-maker whose instrument and voice speak/sing/write the pain; who creates the cries of the heart, mind and soul; who feels the pain,  with lyrics that sing forever in our hearts. Only a human can experience the wonder, the artistry, the sensitivity involved in music-making that contributes to the common and shared values of our humanity.

While various forms of bread or pasta are staples, vegetables are highly seasonal - e.g., collards, turnip greens, chopped cabbage, carrot, squash/zucchini. You also have prepared foods (PBJ, bagels with cheese, occasionally cornbread or even cake) and a variety of dairy -cottage cheese, cream, 1% milk, oat milk.
The pantry operates out of a non-denominationoal church, with an additional outlet at the public library's annex, Their skeletal vollunteer staff would go nuts trying to create bundles for individual families, because the quantities of individual donated items are not even remotely equal. So, it's first-come, first-served.

comments.name: nobody2
comments.body:
Maybe it’s me, and I’m just too old to read rhapsodic reviews of a restaurant decorated in Goodwill shmattas and featuring food that otherwise would be discarded or offered to people who didn’t know any better. Wagyu beef tongue soaked until mushy? Potato starch added to mashed potato? Seaweed dust? 
Perhaps the restaurant could have been named The Emperor’s New Menu. 
Perhaps this is fine dining in the Age of Trump. Believe what I tell you.

comments.name: adrian
comments.body: The food seems a bit studied and idiosyncratic, and not as interesting as the ambience and intangibles Ms Mishan works really hard to infuse into the review.

comments.body: My kind of restaurant!  When I worked in the Broadway-Lafayette part of town back in the nineties the restaurants in the area were like this. When next next we visit we’ll stop by.

comments.name: Carmela Fabietto Stanford
comments.body:
My takeaway from the review itself, the fine print at the bottom of it, and a reading of the menu on the website, is that Somssi has a limited Asian-accented menu with often overly salty food that has an oddball melange of flavors, charges $9 for bread, $13 for fries, has uninteresting desserts, and is noisy. 

To specify one dish, that hardly seems like a true “ragu” with the linguine. This, of course, begs the question: how should we define ragu? 

Reading between the lines, Ms. Mishan seems to be telling us that all of the negative elements are okay if you’re eating with friends. The headline indicates that the restaurant has “just enough appeal” to be worth a visit. Eating with friends or “just enough appeal” doesn’t cut it when there are so many better places to eat in NYC, especially in Manhattan.

comments.name: HANK
comments.body: I guess I will never understand this incessant push to present a dish to a customer that looks like it should be framed rather than eaten. Forget affordability.

comments.name: Barbara Kruger
comments.body: Ligaya, I had to slow down to let your words sink in and had mixed feelings of delight and overload.  If your words were food I would be tempted to overeat and pay the price.

comments.name: Albert
comments.body:
"this is a place where you can spend a delightful evening. There may be only a couple of truly standout dishes. But some nights it’s enough to be with friends in a relaxed, not-too-expensive spot that, in an increasingly cookie-cutter world, has genuine personality and warmth. Shouldn’t we recognize these restaurants too?"

Of course we should. (We? No, you.)

Go to more of them and report back. Less super expensive tasting menus and less hoity-toity and less outré and less buzzy (though Somssi is pretty buzzy), and way more places where we can enjoy a delightful evening and a good meal with friends in a relaxed, not-too-expensive spot with genuine personality and warmth.

That would be appreciated!  (I bet there's a whole lot of them out there in this huge city.)

comments.name: Abigail
comments.body: September 11th to me means a monumental day of remembrance and sorrow for the people whose lives were lost. But, at the same time, I don't know what I'm supposed to feel on my own, only what was taught to me in school. I have no recollection of the event, as I wasn't even alive to hear about it when it happened. I feel like a poser in a way. I'm acting like I'm actually sad for those who were lost, when in reality I don't feel anything. It's numbing and I, as a person, feel horrible for acting like it hurts. I feel horrible for the families of the victims, but since I didn't experience it or lose anyone, I feel indifferent at the same time.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
What does Sept. 11 and its anniversary mean to you? What words, images, thoughts or feelings come to mind when you think of that day?

To me 9/11 and its anniversary means that it is a time of remembrance. I was not not even born when 9/11 had taken place but I understand the impact that it had. Many people lost their lives that day or were scarred physically or mentally.  Even people who didn't even die that day could have lost someone that meant a lot to them like their friends, parents, or even children. Whenever I think of 9/11 one thought that comes to my mind is how scared  the people were. I think about how afraid people were during that day, the confusion and shock that people experienced as the towers were attacked and not knowing what was happening or what to do. I hope that those people who were afraid that day were able to move on and recover from what happened. One feeling that comes to my mind whenever I think about the attack is one of anger. I can imagine that people were angry at what was happening and wanting someone to pay and I can completely understand. The people who caused that attack had no right to decide who gets to live and who gets to die.

comments.name: Rose
comments.body: In my opinion, I feel like 9/11 doesn't mean anything to me personally. My mom apparently witnessed the plane that flew over Cleveland and crashed, which was the lesser-known hijacked plane. Whenever I talk about 9/11, she acts as if her parents had died in it, like crying and getting hysterical; obviously, she didn't know anybody on the planes, though. Now, I'm well aware that she had witnessed a plane crash, and maybe it's because I have extremely low empathy, but I just don't understand how people can be so upset over it if they didn't know anybody personally who was affected by it, in either injury or death. Don't get me wrong, I know it was a horrible day, and something that should definitely be remembered, but I feel like I don't have many feelings about it. Also, I do know more nitty-gritty details about 9/11 than others, and I even know how most countries were affected by it, but I've never been the type to really hold any memorials or such in my own home for 9/11. Obviously, I think about it and how sad it is, but it really just doesn't affect me at all emotionally. I do just wanna say that this day helps me remember to appreciate TSA rather than hate it, because it helps us to never have an incident like this again. It also helps me to remember that our first responders, like firefighters, police officers, and healthcare workers, are awesome at their jobs.

comments.name: Khalil
comments.body: The anniversary of the Sept. 11 attack, to me, holds no value to me as I wasn't born until 9 years later, so from my perspective, I have no reason to be angry for something that didn't outright affect me. I will say the U.S. from what I've seen will never be the same as it once was (for example; The TSA), but I know no life before or immediately after the Attack. I will say I will show support and Hold those who died in and after the attack in Great onor, but that also raises questions of "Why should I hold them In great Regard even if I don't know them?" and the worst Photos I've seen about the Attack, was the "Jumpers", People who: 'had no chance of saving themselves by going down the stairs or elevators, so then they Jumped.' No one should have to jump to their deaths because A group of Terrorist hate the U.S. History of Involvement. Even if it wasn't the U.S., no one should, So I guess that's the strongest feeling or opinion I have on the Sept. 11 Attack.

comments.name: Zariyah
comments.body: While I was not alive during the time period of this event, September 11th holds a significant meaning to me that I should be grateful for every moment I have with my mom. My mom has grew up in New York her whole life, and she almost lost her life when the planes crashed into the Twin Towers. She used to tell me growing up that when it occurred she was only 8 blocks away from the incident. As it was unexpected, she had to drop everything at work and walk through the dust cloud to escape that area. Hearing this story as I got older, it made me think of people crying and in distress, a huge cloud of debris, and everyone was helpless. Whenever the topic comes up, I begin to have a heavy heart for everyone who suffered from those events, both being there and the family of those who were there. The event and aftermath of 9/11 has affected my family by causing them to steer away from riding on planes to travel places, which resulted in my brother and I flying on a plane for the first time in 2018. This not only shaped my family but also my generation in the aspect of security protocols that have to be taken in place and reminds people that not every day is guaranteed.

comments.name: Max G
comments.body: For me Annika Heegaard description most resonates with me. I feel both deeply saddened and disconnected from the event at the same time. No one I personally know was physically affected by 9/11 which causes me to not have a connection with the tragic day. On the other hand, the stories I have heard and videos I have seen in school make me feel strong emotion for the day. My lack of personal connection and stories/videos i have heard or seen cause me to have conflicted levels of care when it comes to 9/11.

comments.name: Nevaeh
comments.body: Growing up 9/11 was a horrific attack retold from every possible point of view, though one person’s has stuck with me. My dad watched 9/11 happen on a screen while sitting in his 10th grade English class, a normal day suddenly turned into a lasting memorial. 9/11 was the biggest event of his childhood but mine has been filled with mass casualty events. I, much like other teenagers, struggle to see September 11 as monumental when I've been growing up in a world filled with violence, death, and divide. I understand the impact and somberness of the September 11 attacks though I struggle to see why the monthly school shootings today are not monumental too.

comments.name: Jeremiah R
comments.body: 9/11 means to me remembering what I didn't go through. I obviously was born years after 9/11, but it still affects us to this day. Lots of people lost family members. To those who didn't lose family members, they saw a traumatic event unfold either in real life or on television. I remember watching hours of footage of the attacks, just appalled at why someone would do that. Why would someone put thousands of lives at danger. The victims that did survive delivered powerful statements that make you feel like you were at the towers on 9/11. Everyone that was alive during the attacks knows where they were on 9/11, thats just how impactful it was towards Americans, but also the world.

At this point, reality has begun to outstrip Hollywood visions. 
Terrifyingly, here's from today's Guardian:

"Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said ... that the industry is falling behind in attempts to deal with [AI's] apocalyptic potential.

“'We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!' Hubinger wrote. 'I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.'

"...A second response came from Samuel Marks, Anthropic’s “scalable oversight lead”, who posted a lengthy analysis he stressed was in his personal capacity:

..."'AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),' wrote Marks. 'This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.'

Look them up on the Times website.  Do what you can to relieve needless suffering.  In doing so, you will stand up for human decency in the face of all that has gone wrong here since Trump took that fateful ride down the escalator ten years ago.  Show this world that his willful ignorance, insufferable greed, unbridled selfishness, and venomous hatred are appalling aberrations in the human psyche.  Rebuke the notion that kindness is a weakness, something Trump learned from his father and that his comrade-in-greed Elon Musk shamelessly promotes. Most of this is the legacy of the Manhattan Project.  What would you rather have?  Forever nuclear waste that is staggeringly expensive to neutralize and store, or them "unsightly" windmills that supply revenue to farmers, or the potential of solar power working in tandem with a farmer's need to shelter animals or shade arable land?  Trump wants his legacy to live on forever after him--maybe we should just rename Hanford the Trump Dump and that would about sum his legacy up.  Congress seems to have abdicated its constitutional sole power of the purse, and Trump--who is picking every pocket his tiny hands can reach into--is just forging ahead spending Other People's Money--much of it yours and mine--on whatever flatters his inflated sense of self.

If only another Michael Douglas were around to profice a Gordon Gekko in a *new* "Wall Street" to say emphatically  "Greed is NOT good"!

"Monetizing" is the word used when everyday people try to turn their skills into businesses. It's the holy grail today - podcasts, videos, tiktoks, becoming an "influencer", all in the hopes of turning a profit and selling us on them, basically. Maybe the grim employment outlook has something to do with the hope to profit off their children's cute words or a pet's antics.

But at the small business level, selling out to corporations is that holy grail. It's why we now have seven to ten major international conglomerates controlling - and profiting from - nearly every commodity bought in stores, from womb to tomb, as it's said. 
I heard recently a small coffee roasting business that had its debut selling at our local farmers market not only boomed, but that they sold to Nestle for over $450 million. Good for the startup, not for us.
Knowing Nestle's history, I was devastated to hear that buying this truly excellent coffee now enriches a company we "boycotted" ever since we heard of its dealings in 1970.  Nestle  convinced poor mothers in underdeveloped countries that their own milk wasn't nutritious enough for their babies and they should buy formula instead. The results were tragic.

So I hope these seaweed farmers can prevail to keep their time-honored businesses and traditions and not need to "sell out".

comments.name: Alphonso Bedoya
comments.body:
The closing of the commons.

This kind of thing has been going on for hundreds of years, first as a way of favoring or placating particular members of aristocracy who had petitioned a monarch with a grievance but now as a feature of extractive capitalism… in a democracy, no less.

As we have seen with 47’s repeated assaults in the courts— be it birthright citizenship, tariffs or mail-in voting— a loss in some awful power grab is only an invitation to try again in some other equally scabrous way.

These folk gathering the goods of the sea, as they have for generations, are right to expect that once this door has been cracked into their way of life there will now be repeated attempts to fling it open all the way.

We’ve gone from rule by divine right to rule by the god-almighty dollar…

… or pound or euro or yen or yuan… it’s all filthy lucre.

Now I gotta go online to check my portfolio…

I’m puzzled as to the LW’s relationship with her stepchildren. I understand she needs to clarify the situation but she married 50 years ago when the children were young. Does she still view them as merely her husband’s children after all these years?  It seems so. Did they not live near them?

While she doesn’t need to repair the relationship between the late father and his son, nor does she need to give all three children an equal amount of, or any money from the estate, please don’t do anything so severely unequal that it will damage the relationship between the siblings. The LW seems to agree that the father probably didn’t treat the middle child as fairly. 

Perhaps you might give a gift from yourself- a special item, reflecting your feelings for this child, separate from the father’s estate.

comments.name: D

Sounds like the 3 children have the possibility of even more inheritance down the road from their mother.  The LW is not obligated to split her assets equally.    If LW can't reconcile herself to a situation of unequal shares of the inheritance, she could keep her condo, sell the house and spend the money while she is still alive.  And decide what to do with HER condo that might not involve any of them.  No one is 'owed' an inheritance.

comments.name: Peter W.
comments.body:
We’ve been going to Stratford almost every year (excluding the Covid calamity) since the middle 1970s and I’m here to state - unequivocally - there is no “better” theater anywhere. Not NYC, not LA, not London, not Paris. To be sure, there is “as good” theater - particularly in NYC but not “better”.

Donna Feore has given us some of the best musicals we’ve ever seen - including one that was missed by this critic - the second rendition of “Something Rotten”. This production was funnier, more imaginative and better danced than the previous one and I predict that this play will be repeated often at Stratford.

We’ll keep going as long as health permits - and as long as Canada keeps letting us in.

Trump is doing everything he possibly can to destroy these wonderful cultural links. It saddens me to think of how long it will take to rebuild them even if post-Trump, we have an administration that tries to do so.

comments.name: Rex
comments.body: Bravo for covering one of the pre-eminent theater venues in the world.  Cimolino has indeed done bravura work by (in effect) rescuing the multi-venue cluster of theaters from financial challenge, Covid, and perhaps (now) public disinterest. Attendance is mult-generational, and should only increase with all the digital marketing, outreach to Canada as a whole, and appeal to states such as mine (Michigan has a long, long history of support for the festival, and will no doubt benefit from enhanced coverage of it and more outreach.) Membership is key-- the starter package gets you into good seats at very reasonable rates.  We enjoyed seven shows in four days, just recently.  The Tempest was poorly mic'd when we were there; I like to hear every, rich, Shakespearean word, please!  The superstar lead in a production requires strong support yet we didn't see (much less hear) that.  Immediate feedback from the audience and addressing of issues would have helped such a situation. Othello was magnificent, as was Midsummer Night's Dream.  The latter is a celebration of the world, for its cast and celebratory grace, on one of Canada's finest stages! Overall, Ontario and Canada are so welcoming and understanding, offering a vacation that we will always treasure. Bravo, Stratford, and let the seasons continue!

comments.name: Ron Davis

It is gratifying to read your framing of the shows you saw, and of the Stratford Festival in general, as one of friendship, forgiveness, resilience and endurance. 

The understandable emotional reactions today to the manufactured hostilities that will surely pass should be tempered by the same spirit that shown to Antonio by Prospero when he says "I do forgive thee, Unnatural though thou art".

comments.name: Helen Shaw
comments.body: Years and years ago I saw a show at the Stratford Festival — Cymbeline, starring Geraint Wyn Davies — and I've been thinking about it ever since. Zeus appeared as an enormous animatronic eagle with red eyes; at one point an entire Roman legion marched through the audience. It was therefore a huge pleasure to return to Stratford and to talk to Antoni Cimolino (who directed that Cymbeline!) about the festival. Stratford feels like art-paradise, not least because the town's life is interbraided with the theater's. At every performance, I saw actors from other shows in the audience, chatting merrily with theatergoers who had clearly been watching their careers for years. A beautiful, calm place, even in the middle of a tornado.

The thing about Shakespeare is that his view of humanity is so magisterial that he can be used to illustrate multiple truths. When I was teaching, 'The Tempest' was interpreted as a post-colonial narrative, focusing on the plight of Caliban, obviously critiquing England's imperialistic (implicitly racist) policies of the day, and the difficulty of rising above your station in the Elizabethan age.

I'd love to see a version of the play that valorizes forgiveness; it would be like discovering 'The Tempest' all over again.

comments.body:
It appears as if the author sees evil as a glitch rather than a feature. Humanity's entire history - both biological and cultural - suggests the opposite. Whatever "evil" entails, it is part of us, coded in our DNA, baked into our behavior. It will not, indeed cannot disappear, no matter how persistently we resist it. 
This is not Thomas Hobbes talking, just me.

comments.name: Kim Messick
comments.body:
Very interesting.
One obvious question, and a possible source of skepticism about the usefulness of the concept of evil, is what distinguishes evil acts (or, more broadly, states of affairs) from the "merely" bad or wrong?
One answer looks to scale: Killing one person is both bad and wrong, say, but killing a million is evil. This doesn't satisfy, though. Torturing a child to death must be evil if anything is, whether it's one child or a dozen. 
A more plausible answer involves a different measure of scale. Here the question is not the number of victims, but the extent to which an act (or state of affairs) negates values fundamental to the moral order. (Or at least to OUR moral order.) On this view, an evil act inverts or effaces an essential ethical element in a way that a merely bad or wrong act does not. It will be tempting to tie this notion to some picture of the agent's intentionality; X commits adultery, aware that it involves bad (and/or wrong) effects, but her principal motivation is simple lust. Her adulterous act is not an attack on the moral order as such. This line of thought has some force, but its emphasis on the intentionality of particular persons could be hard to align with the kind of institutional or systematic evil that Neiman and Arendt rightly want to discuss. 
Food for thought!

articles.title: What Does 9/11 Mean for Those Too Young to Remember It?
articles.summary: Students discuss the significance of the terrorist attacks that they know only as history.

comments.name: David Murdy
comments.body:
I was born in 1962, just a few months before the Cuban Missile Crisis. I too learned of it in history class.  I knew it was serious but couldn't relate to the feelings of those who lived through it or the tenor of the USA.  I think what I and the country felt on, and following 9/11 helped me to understand. It was a feeling of panic and an all-around fear of terrorism. And after the fear started to subside it became a feeling of resolve and patriotism. I wish we were still in those last two across this great land.

JKE

comments.name: Marion Anderson
comments.body: These expressions give me hope for the future of our country.  We are not lost - we are temporarily dislocated.  Twenty-five years of conflict with the enemy who hates us and what we stand for; actually, the current conflict started in Iran forty-seven years ago.  This, too, will pass and there will be a time of relative calm and optimism about the future.

comments.name: William Klein
comments.body:
I am pleased to see that all of the submissions discussed the unity that followed 9/11. But what saddens me is that this unity is far from what is happening in our national landscape today. Having lived 9/11 up close and personal, it seems as if our unity ended just a few short years after that tragic event, and we are not close to coming together for any common cause.

Yes, we have a common identity and a common heritage. But we do not have a common vision. We are heavily divided about the future of this country, and our division is largely driven by fear rather than optimism. Perhaps because so much of what followed 9/11 was done out of fear (fear of another attack, fear of the unknown, fear of others), we seem to have lost what is good in our country and ourselves. IMO, far too many see the future as something from which we must be protected, rather than as challenges that must be seized and managed. We seem to have lost our sense of overcoming instead being replaced by being protected.

I do worry about the future, as someone older. I do worry that in today's America, far too many would let others do the work for them rather than them taking the reigns themselves. Previous generations of Americans looked to challenges as just that; obstacles to be overcome rather than something that should be shunned. I truly hope that I am wrong, but 9/11 IMO shaped this world in some cases the wrong way.

comments.name: D I Shaw
comments.body:
The most important things for those too young to remember 9/11 itself to learn are these: 1) who did it; and 2) why they did it, and apply that knowledge to understanding what is happening in Western Europe and the Anglo-sphere today and what that means for constitutional norms and public policy, thus informing whom they should support politically,

Wearing keffiyehs over tee-shirts with simplistic (often absurd, e.g. Queers for Palestine) slogans and waving fancy placards fresh from Office Depot all paid for by Quataris are likely not their best moves. Neither is voting for leftist dual nationals with questionable loyalties.

We face now, as then, a conundrum. How do we reconcile the freedoms of the West with the openly-stated intentions of immigrants who have no interest in assimilation NOR, most importantly, in pluralism, but rather the goal of eventual domination. 

I have had a long life to think about this, and I wish I were wise enough to know how to thread this needle, to preserve the rights of all to freedom without violating our own principles by shutting down those who would impose their ways on us.  I am not.

However,  how well the young truly understand 9/11 will determine not only how their own lives may turn out, but those of their children and generations to follow.  As WWII was what my generation had to understand, 9/11 is what they must comprehend. They must not forget that,

"There is nothing new in the world except the history you have not read." - Harry S. Truman.

At the Apple Store last night half a dozen soon-to-be-old iPhones in a row showed bits and stills for “Ted Lasso”; I asked the earnest teenaged sales rep if he’d watched it— he had not. I could not resist saying that it was my all-time best show ever (“since the fifties”, said I, to be sure I had his attention), and made noises about football and kindness, redemption, humanness, high-brow Apple TV,… and happily remembered we would get home to see the new episode.
I think Mr Orr’s recap is spot on; there is much to criticize, (e.g. Zelda, weird Beard subplot, Keeley and Rebecca seemingly stuck).  The women players are more of a Greek chorus than fully fleshed-out people, to date. But I have drunk the Lasso Kool-Aid, and think the best is yet to come: Apple Tartt Vodka indeed! Two-eyed Cyclops! Voltron the philosopher!

comments.name: Xoxarle

"a poll for NRK showed that support for the monarchy had risen to 72 percent"

Hard to articulate how bizarre this should read: the concept of a royal family in thrall to public opinion. It shows how uncomfortably they exist in the modern world. These institutions should theoretically exist in defiance of public approval, they represent the imposition of power and privilege, or the illusion thereof, without the need for approval. They aren't elected or re-elected.  

The fact that the Norweigan royals, like their British counterparts, have recent scandals to their name, should tell us they really don't value the implicit bargain with their subjects: that they get to live a life of enormous privilege and public funding in return for representing the nation steadfastly and positively. Often these scandals are a direct result of the entitlement that these institutions breed, making these scandals a self-fulfilling prophesy.

comments.name: The Tennessean
comments.body: I'm surprised data center strain on the electrical grid has not been addressed.  But big business Texas always puts development and money before everything else. Will its voters never learn? Texas runs an independent electrical grid and it's notoriously unreliable. The poorly maintained grid was the cause of about 700 people dying in the hard freeze we had in 2021 when residents lost power for days (I had none for 46 hours) in negative temperatures. ERCOT updated the grid since then but the data centers will likely put it under a lot of strain once again. I shudder to think what may happen in a state that is notorious for severe weather events.
